ideas.name: Inflation and the cost of living

en.text: Inflation is a regular and continuous rise in the general price level, the average price of goods and services; a fall in the price level is deflation. Inflation lowers the purchasing power of money and raises the cost of living. Some governments index wages, contracts and interest rates to inflation; when wages do not keep up, the real wage and living standards fall.

screens.ask: Last year 100 Birr bought 2 kg of sugar. Now the prices of almost everything have risen 25 %. How much sugar does 100 Birr buy now?

ideas.name: The consumer price index and the inflation rate

en.text: The consumer price index (CPI) compares the cost of a typical consumer basket with its cost in a base year: CPI = (current cost ÷ base-year cost) × 100, so the base year is 100. The inflation rate is the percentage change in the CPI: (CPIₜ − CPIₜ₋₁) ÷ CPIₜ₋₁ × 100, always dividing by the past CPI. A negative rate means deflation, as in the book's wheat-and-oil example for 2002 E.C.

am.text: የሸማቾች የዋጋ መለኪያ = የአሁኑ ቅርጫት ዋጋ ÷ የመሠረት ዓመት ዋጋ × 100። የዋጋ ግሽበት መጠን = (የአሁኑ − ያለፈው) ÷ ያለፈው × 100።

screens.title: A basket of goods
screens.ask: A family buys the same basket every year. It cost 200 Birr in 2000 E.C. and 280 Birr in 2001 E.C. By what percent did its cost rise?
screens.after: (280 − 200) ÷ 200 × 100 = 40 %. Tracking a fixed basket is the idea behind the CPI.

screens.title: Inflation from the CPI
screens.ask: Move last year's and this year's CPI. Watch the inflation rate. When is it negative?
screens.note: Inflation = (CPI this year − CPI last year) ÷ CPI last year × 100. A negative rate is deflation.

en.text: By speed, inflation is creeping (3 % or less a year), walking (3 % to under 10 %), running (10–20 %), galloping (double or triple digits) or hyperinflation (more than 50 % a month). By cause, it may be demand-pull, cost-push, or wage, profit, scarcity, deficit, currency, credit or foreign-trade induced. Printing money to finance spending (seigniorage) acts like an inflation tax; Hungary in 1946 and Zimbabwe in 2007–2009 show how far hyperinflation can go.

screens.title: Fifty percent a month
screens.ask: If prices rise 50 % every month, about how many times higher are they after one year?
screens.after: 1.5¹² ≈ 129.7: prices rise about 130-fold in a year. That is hyperinflation.

screens.title: Types by cause
paras: Inflation: too much money chasing too few goods; demand exceeds supply.
Causes: demand-pull, cost-push, wage, profit, scarcity, deficit, currency, credit, foreign trade.
Printing money to finance spending raises the money supply.
This revenue is seigniorage.

screens.title: Extreme cases
paras: Hungary, July 1946: monthly inflation of 41.9 quadrillion percent; prices doubled every 15.3 hours.
Zimbabwe 2007–2009: prices at times doubled daily; a $100 trillion note was printed.
By late 2008 its money was nearly worthless; Zimbabwe adopted the US dollar.
Wars, falling export prices, tax evasion and political stalemate cause large deficits.
